name: 縁（エニ） (Eni)
neighborhood: Yashiro Honmachi (5 min walk from Shimizubashi bus stop, north side of Himeji Castle)
gf_detail: This is a shared-kitchen space with 10+ rotating vendors; no vendor has published gluten-free menus or dedicated allergen information. The building owner is Tanabiki Seimen, a dried-noodle (somen/wheat) manufacturer, and noodle-based dishes are among the offerings. name: 白鷺堂本舗 (Shirasagido Honpo)
gf_detail: This is a mixed wagashi shop — not a dedicated gluten-free establishment. Several products are naturally wheat-free (kuzu mochi, warabi mochi, plain mochi, rice-based daifuku), but wheat-containing items are also sold in the same space: taiyaki and obanyaki use wheat-flour batter, and fu manju (麩まんじゅう) is made from wheat gluten. Mitarashi dango glaze uses soy sauce, which typically contains wheat.

name: spiceスエヒロ (Spice Suehiro)
neighborhood: South of Himeji Castle (10 min walk from Sanyo-Himeji Stn)
gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free menu or certification. The curries are spice-based rather than roux-based, which reduces some GF risk, but no explicit claims are made about wheat-free preparation. Soy sauce (containing wheat) may be used in side items such as hinepon (chicken ponzu) or pickles. Shared kitchen with no stated dedicated fryer or cross-contamination controls. Celiac diners should call ahead

name: ベジタブルカフェ さくらさく (Vegetable Cafe Sakura Saku)
neighborhood: Honmachi (southwest of Himeji Castle, north of Sanyo-Himeji Stn)
gf_detail: No gluten-free menu or labelling exists. The signature dessert — handmade vegetable chiffon cake — is explicitly made with domestic wheat flour, so it is not GF. Soy sauce is used in cooking (the tofu steak glaze is soy-ginger based) and standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat; tamari substitution has not been confirmed.
